ai.title: Supplementary Motor Area
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The SMA coordinates planned, sequential, and bilateral movements. It integrates sensory input and motor plans, influencing execution via corticospinal pathways. Dysfunction leads to motor planning deficits and speech initiation problems.

sections.p: The SMA is part of Brodmann area 6, located on the medial frontal lobe. It works with the premotor cortex and primary motor cortex to plan and initiate movements, especially complex sequences and bilateral actions.

Neurons in the SMA receive input from prefrontal and parietal regions, integrate sensory and contextual information, and send signals through the corticospinal tract to the spinal cord. This allows coordinated, timed muscle activation.

t.b: Detects SMA activation during imagined movement; abnormal patterns suggest SMA dysfunction.
Shows reduced SMA activity in patients with apraxia or speech arrest.

b: Basal ganglia dopamine modulates SMA output
sections.p: SMA activity is modulated by dopaminergic input from the basal ganglia and by cortical feedback. It is suppressed during automatic movements and engaged during novel or complex tasks.

t.b: Improves SMA-mediated motor initiation in Parkinsonian patients.

sections.p: Lesions or dysfunction of the SMA cause motor planning deficits, such as akinetic mutism, speech arrest, and impaired initiation of voluntary movements. In low‑resource settings, stroke, infection, or trauma can damage the SMA.

t.b: Identifies focal lesions in the medial frontal lobe; absence of SMA signal correlates with motor planning deficits.

sections.p: In East African hospitals, SMA dysfunction may present after intracerebral hemorrhage, septic encephalopathy, or HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorders. Recognising speech arrest and movement initiation failure guides imaging and supportive care.

b: SMA: initiation deficit, M1: strength deficit
sections.p: Remember that SMA lesions spare basic reflexes and primary motor output but impair initiation and sequencing. In exams, differentiate SMA from primary motor cortex (M1) by noting preserved muscle strength but absent voluntary initiation.
